text: You have an n by n chessboard. Place n queens so that no two queens attack each other. Return how many different ways you can do it.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two queens attack if they share a row, a column, or a diagonal. And I only need the count, not the boards themselves. Is that right?
Yes. Just the number. You don't need to build any boards.

Got it. One thing I notice right away. There are n queens and n rows, and no two can share a row. So every row has exactly one queen. That means I can place queens row by row, one per step, and the only real choice in each row is the column. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and nine.

Small. So exponential search is fine, as long as I cut dead branches early. Let me run through the example. For n equals four the answer is two. If I write the queen's column for each row, the boards are one, three, zero, two and two, zero, three, one — mirror images of each other. For n equals one, one queen on one cell, so the answer is one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every permutation of columns, one column per row, and then check the diagonals at the end. That's n factorial full boards. It still works for n equals nine, but it builds a lot of boards that were already broken in the second row. This problem reminds me of the classic backtracking template: choose, recurse, un-choose. Here I go row by row, try each column, and skip a column the moment it's attacked. A bad prefix dies right away, so I never build its children.

Here's the plan. One: when the row index reaches n, all rows are filled, so add one. Two: in this row, skip any column that's attacked. Three: mark the column and both diagonals, recurse to the next row, then clear them. Three boolean arrays track which lines are taken, so each check is constant time. One thing worth flagging — the diagonal indexing. On a slash diagonal, r plus c stays the same. On a backslash diagonal, r minus c stays the same, but it can be negative, so I add n minus one. Both arrays need two n minus one slots. And since I only count, I drop the board and keep one int — less memory, and no copies at the leaf. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function sets up the counter and the flag arrays and starts at row zero. The search adds one when the row reaches n; otherwise it tries each free column with mark, recurse, unmark. One thing worth flagging — the row array. I added it for symmetry, but it never does any work. Each level places at most one queen in its own row, so row of r is always false when I read it. Removing it gives the same answers for n from one to nine. And the answer is passed by reference, so every leaf adds into the same counter in the main function.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. n equals four, expected two. The row that matters is the first time we reach row four, on the path starting at column one: all four rows have a queen, so the answer becomes one. Then we return and clear the flags, so that column and its diagonals are free again. The column-two branch finds the mirror board, and the total is two, in seventeen calls — sixteen placements plus the first call. Let's also test with corner cases. n equals one is one. n equals two and three are zero. Nine gives three hundred fifty-two in about half a millisecond. And the sneaky bug: forget to clear the flags, and n equals four returns zero. The un-choose step is required for correctness.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n factorial. Row r has at most n minus r free columns, because each earlier queen takes one column. The diagonal checks cut it down a lot in practice: about eighty-four hundred calls for n equals nine. The space complexity is O of n — the recursion depth plus the flag arrays. I keep no board at all. Oh, one more thing — I'd clean up the code by dropping the row array. It's dead weight, since the recursion level already is the row.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that one queen per row turns this into a column choice per level, and then noticed your own row array was never used. You explained the r minus c plus n minus one shift instead of just writing it. And you showed the un-choose step is a correctness requirement, with n equals four going to zero without it. Good work.
